tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand what @eslint-sets/eslint-config is: a modern ESLint flat-config preset supporting Vue, React, Svelte, Next.js, Nuxt, Astro, Angular, UnoCSS and more. It lists the headline features this tour will trace through the code -- ESLint v9 flat config, FlatConfigComposer chaining, @stylistic integration, TypeScript TypeGen, Prettier support, framework auto-detection, git ignore, and disables. Reading it first gives you the vocabulary and architectural intent before any source file.

tour.title: Package Entry Point
tour.description: src/index.ts is the package barrel that consumers import. It re-exports the default eslintConfig function, all public configuration types, and the FlatConfigComposer from src/configs. This file is the contract between the library and its users -- everything reachable from `import eslintConfig from '@eslint-sets/eslint-config'` originates here. Understanding what it exposes maps directly to the README's advertised public API.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript barrel files use `export * from` and `export { ... } from` to re-export modules, creating a single clean public entry surface. For a config library, the barrel also re-exports types so consumers get both the runtime function and the type-safe options in one import.

tour.title: Type System & Generated Types
tour.description: src/types.ts defines the vocabulary the whole library speaks: the ConfigNames union (selectable preset names), the RuleOptions mapped type, and the Linter type aggregating all framework rule sets. It has one of the highest fan-in counts (25 dependents), so every config module depends on these definitions. Alongside it, src/typegen.d.ts is the auto-generated 19k-line ambient declaration file backing the README's 'TypeScript TypeGen' feature -- it gives rule keys literal-string autocomplete and type-checking.
tour.languageLesson: Ambient `.d.ts` declaration files augment the global type space without emitting runtime code. When generated from installed ESLint plugins, they turn loosely-typed rule names like `'no-unused-vars'` into literal-string unions, enabling autocompletion and compile-time validation of rule keys across every framework config.

tour.title: Shared Constants & Glob Patterns
tour.description: src/constants.ts is the most depended-upon file in the project (fan-in 29). It centralizes file glob patterns (GLOB_*), framework package lists (VUE_PACKAGES, NEXTJS_PACKAGES, etc.), and editor environment constants. Because every config and plugin module imports these, changing a glob or framework signature here propagates consistently across the whole preset. This is the foundational layer the rest of the config assembly reads from.

tour.title: Plugin Auto-Detection
tour.description: src/plugins.ts implements the README's headline 'auto-detection of installed frameworks'. It provides has* checks (hasVue, hasReact, hasSvelte, hasNextjs, ...) backed by loadPlugin for dynamic imports with graceful failure. The detection logic reads the package lists from Step 4 against the user's installed dependencies, so the composer in Step 7 can decide which framework configs to activate without manual toggles.
tour.languageLesson: Dynamic plugin loading uses `await import('eslint-plugin-x')` inside try/catch, returning null on failure. This optional-dependency pattern lets a preset support many frameworks without forcing users to install all of them -- if the package isn't present, the plugin simply isn't loaded and its rules never activate.

tour.title: Config Assembly Utilities
tour.description: src/utils/index.ts supplies the mechanical helpers that assemble flat configs: renamePlugin for plugin-key renaming, deep merge for combining layered rule sets, environment detection, and option resolution. With fan-out 19 and fan-in 4, it sits in the middle of the dependency graph -- imported by the composer and the individual configs. These utilities are what make the FlatConfigComposer chaining methods (append/prepend/renamePlugins) from the README work correctly.
tour.languageLesson: Deep-merging arrays of config objects is non-trivial: later entries override earlier rule values while plugin arrays are concatenated. ESLint flat config resolves configs in array order, so the merge function must preserve that ordering to let users override presets via `.append()` without silent rule conflicts.

tour.title: The Config Composer
tour.description: src/configs/index.ts is the orchestrator and the heart of the library -- it has the highest fan-out (47) of any file, importing every individual framework, language, and tooling config. Based on the user's options and the auto-detection results from Step 5, it assembles the right subset into a single flat config array wrapped in a FlatConfigComposer. This is where the README's FlatConfigComposer chaining API (.append()/.prepend()/.renamePlugins()) is returned to the caller.
tour.languageLesson: FlatConfigComposer wraps a config array and exposes chainable mutation methods. Each `.append()` / `.prepend()` returns a new composer instance, enabling immutable-style composition: `eslintConfig({}).append(rules).prepend(globals)`. The composer is what the README means by 'FlatConfigComposer Chaining'.

tour.title: Framework Configs
tour.description: These three modules are representative of the per-framework config family under src/configs/. vue.ts dynamically loads eslint-plugin-vue and the vuejs-accessibility plugin with block processors for script/style/template. react.ts conditionally enables react, react-hooks, and react-refresh based on detected packages. typescript.ts assembles type-aware linting rules driven by the project's TypeScript options. Each follows the same factory pattern: detect, load, configure, return a config object the composer merges.

tour.title: Stylistic & Prettier Integration
tour.description: These two modules implement the README's formatting features. stylistic.ts wraps @stylistic/eslint-plugin with configurable indent, quotes, and JSX/TSX formatting plus sensible defaults -- the '@stylistic Integration' headline feature. prettier.ts disables the conflicting ESLint formatting rules when Prettier is the chosen formatter, the 'Prettier Support (optional)' feature. Together they encode the stylistic-vs-Prettier choice surfaced in the basic-usage guide.
tour.languageLesson: ESLint and Prettier overlap on formatting rules. The conventional fix is for the Prettier integration to mark stylistic rules as 'off', delegating formatting to Prettier while leaving code-quality rules to ESLint. @stylistic keeps formatting inside the linter for users who prefer a single tool.

tour.title: Ignores & Disables
tour.description: These two small configs deliver two more README features. ignores.ts merges user-provided ignore glob patterns into a single flat-config ignore entry -- the 'Git Ignore Support' feature. disables.ts turns off conflicting or unwanted rules across file types and globs to prevent formatter/linter conflicts -- the 'Disables Support' feature. They run late in the composed array so the disables take precedence over earlier rule sets.

tour.title: CLI Scaffolding Wizard
tour.description: src/cli/index.ts implements an interactive scaffolding wizard that generates an eslint.config.ts file for a project. It walks the user through project type, TypeScript, framework, accessibility, formatter, and additional options (types defined in src/cli/types.ts), then resolves the right dependencies. This is the 'getting started' path documented in docs/guide/cli.md and maps to the README's 'Highly Configurable' claim -- the CLI turns human choices into the typed options Step 7's composer consumes.

tour.title: Dogfooding, Packaging & CI
tour.description: The tour closes with how the project ships and validates itself. eslint.config.ts is the project's own flat config that applies eslint-sets to lint its own source -- the library eats its own dog food. package.json declares the published config, CLI bin entry, build scripts, and dependencies (the 'Project Configuration' layer). The ci.yml GitHub Actions workflow runs lint, typecheck, test, and build on every push and PR, guaranteeing the preset stays green before release. Together these show how a config library is packaged, self-checked, and continuously delivered.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows use `on` for triggers, `jobs` for parallel groups, and `steps` for sequential execution. A typical config-library CI runs typecheck, lint (using the library on itself), test, and build as gating steps before publish -- the dogfooding step doubles as an integration test of the preset's own rules.
